name: Averroes
info: Averroes (Ibn Rushd, 1126–1198) was an Andalusian jurist, judge, physician and philosopher of Córdoba, remembered for his commentaries on Aristotle, his defence of philosophy in Islam and his influence on Jewish and Latin Christian thought.

facts.born: 14 April 1126 (520 AH) in Córdoba, into a family well known for public service in legal and religious fields; grandson of the chief judge of Córdoba
facts.died: 11 December 1198 (9 Safar 595), shortly after returning to court in Marrakesh; first buried in North Africa, his body later moved to Córdoba for another funeral
facts.role: Qadi (judge) of Seville (1169, again 1179) and of Córdoba (1171); court physician to the Almohads (from 1182); chief qadi of Córdoba (1182)
facts.known: his long, middle and short commentaries on Aristotle; the Decisive Treatise on philosophy and revelation; the Incoherence of the Incoherence against al-Ghazali; the Bidāyat al-Mujtahid on differences between the schools of law; the medical Kulliyat (Colliget); Latin Averroism

t: Born in 1126 into a family of Córdoba judges, Averroes (Abū l-Walīd Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad Ibn Rushd) served the Almohad caliphs as judge and physician and wrote commentaries on nearly all of Aristotle's surviving works at a caliph's request.

In the Decisive Treatise he argued that philosophy cannot contradict revelation in Islam, since both are methods of reaching the truth and "truth cannot contradict truth", and he answered al-Ghazali's attack on philosophy in the Incoherence of the Incoherence.

A tribunal in Córdoba condemned his teachings and banished him in 1195, but his commentaries, translated into Hebrew and Latin, reached Jewish and Christian scholars, while his influence in the Islamic world remained modest until modern times.
dyk: Averroes wrote commentaries on nearly all of Aristotle's surviving works; the exception was the Politics, which he could not obtain, so he wrote on Plato's Republic instead.
ev: Born in Córdoba on 14 April, the year his grandfather, the city's chief judge, died
In Marrakesh, capital of the Almohad Caliphate, makes astronomical observations and supports the building of new colleges
Introduced by Ibn Tufayl to the caliph Abu Yaqub Yusuf, begins his Aristotle commentaries and is appointed qadi of Seville
Writes the Decisive Treatise on the compatibility of Islam and philosophy
Succeeds Ibn Tufayl as court physician and is appointed chief qadi of Córdoba
Tried by a tribunal in Córdoba, which condemns his teachings, orders his works burned and banishes him to Lucena
Dies on 11 December, shortly after returning to court in Marrakesh
The Bishop of Paris condemns 15 doctrines, many of them Aristotelian or Averroist

sections.early:
Averroes, known in Arabic as Ibn Rushd, was born Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Rushd on 14 April 1126 (520 AH) in Córdoba. Little is known of his early life. His family was well known in the city for public service, especially in legal and religious fields. His grandfather Abu al-Walid Muhammad (d. 1126) was chief judge (qadi) of Córdoba and imam of its Great Mosque under the Almoravids, and his father Abu al-Qasim Ahmad was also chief judge until the Almoravids were replaced by the Almohads in 1146. A nickname, al-Hafid ("the Grandson"), distinguishes him from his grandfather.

According to his traditional biographers, his education was "excellent". It began with hadith, jurisprudence, medicine and theology. He learned Maliki jurisprudence under al-Hafiz Abu Muhammad ibn Rizq and hadith with Ibn Bashkuwal, a student of his grandfather, and his father taught him jurisprudence, including Imam Malik's Muwatta, which he memorised. He studied medicine under Abu Jafar Jarim al-Tajail, who probably taught him philosophy too, and he knew the works of Ibn Bajjah (Avempace).

He also studied the kalam theology of the Ash'ari school, which he criticised later in life. His 13th-century biographer Ibn al-Abbar said he was more interested in law and its principles than in hadith and was especially competent in khilaf, the disputes of Islamic jurisprudence. Ibn al-Abbar also mentioned his interest in "the sciences of the ancients", probably Greek philosophy and science.
sections.rise:
Averroes joined a regular meeting of philosophers, physicians and poets in Seville, attended by Ibn Tufayl, Ibn Zuhr and the future caliph Abu Yusuf Yaqub. By 1153 he was in Marrakesh, capital of the Almohad Caliphate, to make astronomical observations and to support the Almohad project of building new colleges. He hoped to find physical laws of astronomical movements and not only the mathematical laws then known, but this research was unsuccessful. He likely met Ibn Tufayl, author of Hayy ibn Yaqdhan and court physician, and the two became friends despite differences in their philosophies.

In 1169 Ibn Tufayl introduced him to the Almohad caliph Abu Yaqub Yusuf. In an account reported by the historian 'Abd al-Wahid al-Marrakushi, the caliph asked whether the heavens had existed since eternity or had a beginning. Averroes, knowing the question was controversial and fearing danger, did not answer. The caliph set out the views of Plato, Aristotle and Muslim philosophers and discussed them with Ibn Tufayl, which put Averroes at ease, and he then gave his own view. He later said the caliph had "a profuseness of learning I did not suspect".

He remained in the caliph's favour until the caliph died in 1184. When the caliph complained to Ibn Tufayl that Aristotle was hard to understand, Ibn Tufayl recommended Averroes to explain him. His first works on the subject date from 1169, and in the same year he was appointed qadi of Seville.
sections.deeds:
As qadi he decided cases and gave fatwas based on religious law. He became qadi of Córdoba in 1171 and of Seville again in 1179, and in 1182 succeeded Ibn Tufayl as court physician; later that year he was appointed chief qadi of Córdoba, an office his grandfather had held. His writing rate rose despite these duties and his travels in the Almohad empire. In law he mostly followed the Maliki school, dominant in al-Andalus, but sometimes rejected the argument of the "consensus of the people of Medina". His Bidāyat al-Mujtahid explains the differences between the Sunni schools of law and why they are inevitable.

He wrote commentaries on nearly all of Aristotle's surviving works, in three kinds: short, middle and long. Only the Physics, Metaphysics, On the Soul, On the Heavens and Posterior Analytics had all three. Among his own treatises, the Decisive Treatise (1178) argues that revelation and philosophy are two methods of reaching the truth, so that scripture which seems to contradict reason must be interpreted allegorically by those "rooted in knowledge". In 1179 he criticised the Ash'arites in the Exposition of the Methods of Proof, and in 1180 he answered al-Ghazali's Incoherence of the Philosophers in the Incoherence of the Incoherence.

In medicine he wrote the Kulliyat (Colliget) around 1162, and described stroke as produced by the brain and the signs of what resembles Parkinson's disease.
sections.opponents:
Averroes criticised his predecessors. He faulted al-Farabi for merging Plato and Aristotle and for misreading Aristotelian logic, and he argued that Avicenna's theory of emanation had fallacies and was not found in Aristotle. He answered al-Ghazali, who had charged the philosophers with unbelief, by saying that many of his criticisms applied only to Avicenna and not to Aristotle.

In 1195 his fortune reversed. Various charges were made against him, and a tribunal in Córdoba condemned his teachings, ordered his works burned and banished him to nearby Lucena. Early biographers pointed to a possible insult to the caliph in his writings. The Encyclopaedia of Islam said the caliph distanced himself from Averroes to win the support of more orthodox ulema, whom he needed for his war against Christian kingdoms, and Majid Fakhry wrote that pressure from traditional Maliki jurists played a part.

Abbas Mahmoud al-Aqqad argued that the causes were political and personal. He noted that Averroes lacked diplomatic tact and had called the caliph the "King of the Berbers" in a commentary on zoology, and that his friendship with the caliph's brother Abu Yahya, governor of Córdoba, aroused suspicion in wartime. Mohammed Abed al-Jabri held that he was punished for condemning tyranny in his commentary on Plato's Republic. The campaign was wider than Averroes: the authorities also burned foundational Maliki texts such as the Mudawwana of Sahnun and banned the study of applied jurisprudence.
sections.last:
Al-Aqqad held that the caliph pardoned Averroes and restored him to favour as soon as the political tensions eased. After a few years Averroes returned to court in Marrakesh and was again in the caliph's favour. The caliph was Abu Yusuf Yaqub, who had succeeded Abu Yaqub Yusuf in 1184.

Averroes died shortly afterwards, on 11 December 1198 (9 Safar 595 in the Islamic calendar). He was first buried in North Africa. His body was later moved to Córdoba for another funeral, which the future Sufi mystic and philosopher Ibn Arabi (1165–1240) attended.

In his astronomy, Averroes had criticised the Ptolemaic system, rejecting eccentrics and epicycles, and had tried to reconcile astronomy with the physics of Aristotle. Later in life he declared that this attempt had failed and said he had neither the time nor the knowledge to reconcile the observed planetary motions with Aristotelian principles. He also said of the astronomy of his time that it "offers no truth, but only agrees with the calculations and not with what exists." The astronomer Nur ad-Din al-Bitruji (d. 1204) adopted most of his reform principles and proposed an early astronomical system based on Aristotelian physics.
sections.legacy:
His legacy in the Islamic world was modest. Part of the reason was geography, as he lived in the far west of Islamic civilisation, and his focus on Aristotle was outdated in the 12th-century Muslim world, which had scrutinised Aristotle since the ninth century and was engaging with newer schools, especially that of Avicenna. In the 19th century, during the Al-Nahda, Muslim thinkers began to engage with his works again as an inspiration to modernise Muslim intellectual tradition.

Jewish scholars received him eagerly. Maimonides (d. 1204) said Averroes "was extremely right". Joseph Ibn Kaspi translated his commentaries on Aristotle's Organon in 1232, and in 1260 Moses ibn Tibbon published translations of almost all his commentaries and some medical works. Jewish Averroism peaked in the 14th century.

In Latin Christendom Michael Scot began translating the long commentaries in 1217, and Averroes became known simply as "The Commentator". The Latin Averroists, among them Siger of Brabant and Boethius of Dacia, centred on Paris and Padua. In 1270 the Bishop of Paris, Étienne Tempier, condemned 15 doctrines, and in 1277 he condemned 219 theses drawn mainly from Aristotle and Averroes. Thomas Aquinas relied on Averroes's reading of Aristotle but attacked his theory that all humans share one intellect. Averroism kept a following until the 16th century. Dante placed him in the first circle of hell, and Raphael painted him in The School of Athens.

summary: Averroes (Ibn Rushd, 1126–1198) was a judge and physician of Córdoba who served the Almohad caliphs and wrote commentaries on Aristotle. He argued that philosophy and revelation agree, was briefly banished in 1195, and through Hebrew and Latin translations shaped Jewish and Christian thought.
references: Roger Arnaldez, Averroes: A Rationalist in Islam (University of Notre Dame Press, 2000)
Majid Fakhry, Averroes (Ibn Rushd) His Life, Works and Influence (Oneworld Publications, 2001)
Ernest Renan, Averroès et l'Averroïsme: Essai Historique (Calmann-Lévy, 1882)
Richard C. Taylor, Averroes: religious dialectic and Aristotelian philosophical thought (Cambridge University Press, 2005)
notes: Death place: the article gives no place of death; it says he returned to court in Marrakesh, died shortly afterwards, and was first buried in North Africa. The 'died' fact says only that.
Aquinas's critique On the Unity of the Intellect is dated 1229 in the article, when Aquinas could hardly have written it; the year is left out.

The article says the caliph was al-Mansur in one place (Encyclopaedia of Islam) and Abu Yusuf Yaqub elsewhere; the text uses Abu Yusuf Yaqub only. The 'last' section's first sentence attributes the pardon to al-Aqqad; read it for wording.

Retina and Parkinson's: the article says he 'might have been' first to identify the retina and that modern scholars dispute what he meant; this is left out of the text. Parkinson's is told as 'what resembles'.
Astronomy and the failed reform are placed under 'last' because the article says 'later in his life'; the date is not given.
Event 1270 is a posthumous event, used as the last 'great change after' the life.
